Chapter 1: The Birth of Art

Key ideas

  • Oldest human remains were found in Africa, especially East Africa.
  • When did humans intentionally start making art? In the Paleolithic, about 40,000 to 30,000 BCE. In Western cultures, "art" must be made or changed by human hands. The Makapansgat pebble (ca. 3,000,000 BCE) looks like a face, so whether it is "art" depends on the culture and time period.
  • What kind of art? Small portable art (jewelry, small paintings, statuettes) because people lived a nomadic lifestyle, plus cave wall paintings.
  • Most common animals: horses, bison (buffalo), woolly mammoths, ibexes.
  • Why profile view? The side view shows more of the animal's body, so it is the most recognizable.
  • Why women more than men? The oldest images of women refer to goddesses or fertility figures; fertility meant survival (Venus of Willendorf has emphasized breasts, belly and hips for pregnancy and childbirth).
  • Why paint caves? No writing yet, so these are educated guesses: people show what matters in their environment. Animals had special or magical power, or were needed for food, clothing and survival, and for living in harmony with nature.
  • Altamira was found in 1879 by Don Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola and his daughter Maria in Santander, Spain.
  • Hall of the Bulls: largest animal in prehistoric art (bull is 11 ft 6 in). Shows twisted perspective: body in profile, head turned so you see both horns.
  • Negative hand imprints (Pech-Merle): painter outlines their hand on the wall; probably a kind of signature.

The three Stone Ages

AgeDatesWhat defines it
Paleolithic (Old Stone Age)40,000 to 9000 BCEOldest sculptures and paintings. Hunting and gathering. Nomadic.
Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age)9000 to 8000 BCEStill hunting, gathering, nomadic. Warmer climate and melting ice in Northern Europe; woolly mammoth disappears.
Neolithic (New Stone Age)ca. 8000 to 2300 BCEMost important age. Agriculture and domesticated animals lead to permanent settlements, cities, social structures, and monumental art and architecture. Human figures become more important.

Prehistoric means before the invention of writing. Nomadic means moving around constantly for food, water and shelter.

Neolithic sites

  • Jericho tower (ancient Palestine, 8000 to 7000 BCE): stone, 30 ft high, to protect a permanent settlement from invaders.
  • Ain Ghazal figures (Jordan): plaster inlaid with cowrie shell (eyes) and bitumen (pupils, outlines). Three or more materials = mixed media. About 35 were ritually buried.
  • Çatal Höyük (Turkey): Neolithic residential complex. Deer Hunt mural shows hierarchal of scale (deer bigger than men) and gender roles (only men hunt).
  • Stonehenge (Salisbury Plain, Wiltshire, England): possibly a cremation/funerary site, solar calendar, observatory, ritual place, healing center. Terms: megalithic, trilithon, post and lintel, henge.

Chapter 2: Ancient Near East (Mesopotamia)

Mesopotamia = "land between two rivers," the Tigris (north) and Euphrates (south). Heart of it is Iraq; also Anatolia (Turkey) and Syria. The Fertile Crescent is the river valley between them.

Why so many cultures? Different groups built civilizations there, and constant war and conquest between independent city states (a city with its own ruler and government). So yes, warfare was common.

CultureFromDatesMust know
SumeriansIraq3500 to 2332 BCEFirst city states, cuneiform, the wheel, irrigation canals, Epic of Gilgamesh, ziggurat temples
AkkadiansIraq2332 to 2150 BCEFirst empire. Rulers demanded loyalty to themselves (not city states) and showed themselves as divine
Neo-SumeriansIraq2150 to 2004 BCEDrove out the Gutians. Gudea of Lagash, diorite statues, Ziggurat at Ur
BabyloniansIraq1894 to 1595 BCEHammurabi and his 282 laws
HittitesTurkey1595 to 1180 BCEConquered Babylon. Lion Gate at Hattusa
AssyriansN. Iraq900 to 605 BCEFierce military, huge empire, lamassus, war and hunting reliefs
Neo-BabyloniansIraq605 to 559 BCENebuchadnezzar II, Ishtar Gate, hanging gardens
PersiansIran559 to 330 BCECyrus, Darius I, Xerxes, Persepolis. Largest empire by 480 BCE

Answers to the guide questions

  • Why temples? Mesopotamians were polytheistic. They built ziggurat temples (mud brick) to worship deities, give offerings in the cella, and pray for abundance, health, and protection.
  • Ziggurat = the huge platform; the small temple sits on top. White Temple at Uruk is dedicated to Anu, the sky god.
  • Social stratification = different levels of wealth, power and status. Only rulers, their families, priests and scribes could enter temples.
  • Inanna = Sumerian goddess of love and war, later called Ishtar; most important female deity.
  • Composite view = head and feet in profile, torso frontal. Composite form = human plus animal combined. Do not mix these up.
  • Stele = large stone slab honoring a ruler's accomplishments, a god, or marking a grave. Stele of the Vultures: Eannatum of Lagash defeats Umma; vultures carry off severed heads on the back.
  • Hierarchal of scale = most important figure is shown largest.
  • Woolley (British, 1920s) excavated the Royal Cemetery at Ur: Standard of Ur, bull headed harp, cylinder seals. He and others took objects to European museums (British Museum).
  • Cylinder and stamp seals: rolled or pressed into clay to make an impression (sign or secure documents and goods). Cylinder seals were a high status symbol worn on bracelets or necklaces. Pu-abi's is lapis lazuli.
  • Lapis lazuli: deep blue stone from Afghanistan, valued like gold by the elite.
  • Sumerians vs Akkadians: Akkadian rulers demanded absolute loyalty to themselves and presented themselves as divine (Naram-Sin's horned helmet, placed close to the sky).
  • Gudea: Neo-Sumerian ruler of Lagash who rebuilt temples, showing piety (clasped hands, temple plan on lap). Diorite = expensive, hard, dark gray stone from Oman.
  • Hammurabi stele (basalt): sun god Shamash hands Hammurabi a rod and ring (builder's tools of civilization). Meaning: the god approves his 282 laws, so divine authority / divine right to rule.
  • Hittite Lion Gate: 7 ft lions as guardian figures protecting the fortified capital Hattusa.
  • Assyrian palace reliefs: warfare and hunting, tied to men, power, strategy and bravery, to show the king's power. No women because of patriarchy (male dominated power) and gender roles: these activities were defined as masculine.
  • Lamassu = winged, human headed bull (composite form), almost 14 ft, guarding palaces; meant to cause fear and awe.
  • Ishtar Gate (Nebuchadnezzar II, blue glazed brick): bulls = Adad (storms), dragons = Marduk and his son Nabu; lions of Ishtar along the processional way. Shows syncretism: the same goddess worshipped across cultures.
  • Persepolis (Darius I and Xerxes): royal citadel, political, ceremonial and administrative center; apadana audience hall with 36 columns; reliefs of conquered nations bringing gifts. Damaged by Alexander the Great (4th c. BCE) as revenge for the Persians damaging the Athenian Acropolis.
  • Syncretism = mixing or blending of religious, cultural or artistic influences. Modern example from the slides: The Citadel shopping center in the City of Commerce copies Assyrian lamassus.

More detail by culture

  • Sumerian economy: wheat cultivation was the basis of the economy and brought great wealth; wheat was traded for other foods, precious stones like lapis lazuli, and cloth. Barley was used to make beer. On the Warka Vase: top register Inanna (largest) greeted by a man with offerings, priest behind her; middle register men carrying wheat and barley; third register alternating female sheep and male rams (fertility, domestication); bottom register wheat growing from soil above wavy lines (the life giving Tigris and Euphrates).
  • Epic of Gilgamesh: about 5,000 years old, credited by Western historians as the oldest written story. Gilgamesh, king of the city state of Uruk, defeats the monster Humbaba, realizes death is inevitable, and gives up searching for eternal life to focus on his life, family and enjoyment on earth.
  • Scribes = royal note takers who also produced business and administrative documents; they were elite and could enter temples.
  • Standard of Ur: a box probably attached to a pole for a military procession or ceremony. War side: top, the ruler (largest) receives captured enemies; middle, uniformed soldiers lead captives; bottom, four chariots pulled by donkeys trample enemies. Peace side: top, the ruler drinks with his court, entertained by a lyre player and a singer (a court eunuch); middle, men (perhaps merchants) bring animals and fish; bottom, peasants carry supplies for the feast. Materials teach us about location, time period, elite taste, and artists' techniques.
  • Bull headed harp (tomb of Pu-abi): gold bull face with lapis lazuli hair and beard; the sound box below shows four square animal scenes.
  • Why Sumer fell to Akkad: Sumerians neglected their lands and agricultural care, wheat production dropped, and their weakened economy left them open to invasion. The Akkadians in central Iraq then built the oldest empire in Mesopotamia.
  • Naram-Sin ruled 2254 to 2218 BCE. On his stele two captured Lullubi (from Iran) beg for their lives, one dead soldier lies under his foot and another falls into a crevice, and two rows of Akkadian soldiers march below. Like the Stele of the Vultures, it connects art, power, politics and propaganda.
  • Neo-Sumerians: around 2150 BCE the Gutians from Iran defeated the Akkadians; the Sumerians rebuilt their army, drove the Gutians out, and Sumerian power returned, so they are called "Neo" (new) Sumerians. Gudea ruled Lagash 2150 to 2125 BCE. The Ziggurat at Ur (ca. 2100 BCE) is mud brick with bitumen at the base to stop leaks and flooding (bitumen was also used on roofs and under boats).
  • Hammurabi ruled 1792 to 1750 BCE. Achievements: conquests that expanded the Babylonian Empire, a re-established centralized government, and 282 laws controlling all parts of society, carved in cuneiform on the lower half of the stele.
  • Hittites: around 1595 BCE they conquered Babylon, then returned home to Anatolia. Capital: Hattusa, a fortified city. Lions guard entrances in many world cultures.
  • Assyrians: empire from the Tigris in Iraq to the Nile in Egypt and from the Persian Gulf to Turkey. Sargon II's citadel at Dur Sharrukin had royal buildings, hundreds of courtyards, religious and ceremonial spaces, and many lamassus. Constant warfare eventually drained their economy and military, and the Neo-Babylonians took over. Assyrian reliefs are low relief in gypsum (a lighter brown, softer stone). Ashurbanipal's lion hunt shows lions attacking his chariot and being speared.
  • Neo-Babylonians: Nebuchadnezzar II ruled 605 to 562 BCE and made Babylon one of the most beautiful cities in the world, with hanging gardens. The Ishtar Gate is in the Staatliche Museen, Berlin.
  • Persians: Persia (Iran) lay east of Mesopotamia and included Elam, Susa, the Zagros Mountains, Bishapur, Persepolis and Media. Cyrus founded the Achaemenid Dynasty and ruled 559 to 529 BCE; he traced his family back to the mythical king Achaemenes to claim the divine right to rule. Cyrus captured Babylon in 539 BCE; the Persians captured Egypt in 525 BCE; by 480 BCE they had the largest empire in the world (most of the Middle East, parts of South Asia and northeastern Europe). Darius I ruled 522 to 486 BCE and Xerxes 486 to 465 BCE. The dynasty lasted until 330 BCE, when Alexander the Great defeated Darius III.
  • Empire = several conquered territories ruled by an emperor. Imperial = the emperor, the empress, their family, and anything related to power within their empire.
  • Persepolis was a "royal citadel" on a high plateau surrounded by heavy walls; it used Assyrian style lamassus (syncretism). The apadana could hold thousands of guests. The processional frieze shows men from conquered nations in their traditional clothing bringing traditional gifts to the emperor.
  • Where objects are now: many Mesopotamian objects are in the Louvre (Paris), the British Museum (London) and Berlin, not in Iraq. The Warka Vase is in the National Museum of Iraq, Baghdad.

Mesopotamian deities

Anu (sky, Uruk, main Sumerian god) · Enlil (winds, earth) · Inanna/Ishtar (love and war) · Nanna (moon, Ur) · Utu/Shamash (sun, justice) · Ningirsu (Girsu) · Marduk (chief Babylonian god, dragon) · Nabu (writing, wisdom, dragon) · Adad (storms, bull)

Chapter 3: Egypt (Kemet) and Nubia

  • Kemet = original name of ancient Egypt, meaning "The Black Land" (the dark fertile soil of the Nile). Using it recognizes Egypt as an African civilization.
  • How Western scholars treated Egypt (professor's notes): they separated Egypt from Africa, called it "Near East" or treated its achievements as "Western," a racist view tied to the slave trade (from the early 1500s) and European colonialism. Museums still separate Egyptian art from African art. Many objects were taken to the British Museum (London), the Louvre (Paris) and the Egyptian Museum in Berlin. Napoleon's 1799 expedition damaged the Sphinx's face because he did not believe Egypt was African.
  • Professor's notes on North Africa: most African art history courses skip North Africa (at UCLA you would study it in "Middle Eastern Studies"). Three reasons: 1) racism from European colonialism, a refusal to see Africa as a united whole or to credit African achievements; 2) by the early 8th century Arabs from the Middle East had conquered North Africa, bringing Arab cultures, Islam and their arts, so today Islam and Arabic are dominant there after more than 1,200 years; 3) Western scholars removed North Africa from the map of Africa and labeled it "Middle Eastern" and "Arab." Before the Arabs, ancient Greeks and Romans also invaded parts of North Africa. The original inhabitants of the whole continent were Indigenous Africans.
  • Colonialism: European colonialism ran from the 16th through the 19th centuries. The slave trade started in the early 1500s with the Portuguese. Westerners called sub Saharan Africa "Black and African" and lands north of the Sahara "Middle Eastern" or "Arab." Europeans shifted from admiring African achievements to calling African cultures "primitive," "uncivilized" and "tribal" through a racist lens. Thousands of objects were stolen and sold to European museums in the 18th and 19th centuries, out of their original cultural context. England and France were the most powerful colonizers, which is why so much African art is in the British Museum and the Louvre; Germany (Berlin) was another colonizer. Keep asking: is the object in Africa, or owned by a European or US museum?
  • The Nile: longest river in the world, flows through Ethiopia (starts there), Nubia (Sudan), and Egypt. Close to Mesopotamia, so there is syncretism (composite view and composite form appear in both).
  • Culture traits: matrilineal (power passes through the mother's side), divine kingship, fertility in art, polytheistic, ancestor worship.
  • Social stratification: pharaoh at the top (political, religious and social leader, divine blood), then priests and elite such as scribes and nobles, then commoners. Tomb chapels were only for the wealthy; most people had simple graves.

Deities

GodRole and symbol
Amun / AmenSupreme god
Re / RaSun god. Symbol: ben-ben stone shaped like a pyramid. Center of worship: Heliopolis (City of the Sun)
OsirisGod of civilization and the afterlife. Pharaohs became him when dead. Green face, white clothing
IsisWife of Osiris, mother of Horus. Fertility, motherhood, female beauty
HorusFalcon god, protector of the pharaoh. Pharaohs were linked to him while alive
HathorCow goddess, nourishes the pharaoh with her milk. Fertility, music, dance
AnubisJackal headed god of mummification
ThothIbis headed god of writing and wisdom; records the heart judgment
MaatGoddess of justice; her feather is weighed against the heart

Timeline

PeriodDatesWorks
Predynastic / Early Dynastic3500 to 2575 BCEPalette of Narmer, Djoser (Dynasty III)

Tombs and the afterlife

  • Mastaba = oldest Egyptian stone tomb style: a flat rectangular platform over a shaft to the burial chamber, with a chapel and a serdab.
  • Djoser's Stepped Pyramid, Saqqara, Dynasty III, by architect Imhotep: mastabas stacked on top of each other. One of the oldest monumental stone buildings in history. Fluted stone columns (later adopted by the Greeks) and papyrus columns (symbol of Lower Egypt).
  • Saqqara = funerary city on the west bank of the Nile (west = sunset = death). Tombs face east, where the sun rises.
  • Why the pyramid shape? In Dynasty 4 the cult of the sun god Re at Heliopolis grew. His symbol was the pyramid shaped ben-ben stone, so pharaohs changed from mastabas to pyramids.
  • Great Pyramids at Gizeh: left Menkaure (son), middle Khafre (father of Menkaure), right Khufu (father of Khafre).
  • Great Sphinx: composite form (man and crouching lion), wears the royal nemes, guards the whole funerary complex; lions guard the rising and setting sun.
Heads up: the exam guide lists mummification, ka, canopic jars and amulets, but those details are not in the slide files you sent. They are likely in your lecture notes. The basics below are standard art history facts, so check them against your notes.
  • Ka = the life force or spirit double that lives on after death. It needs a preserved body or a statue as a home, which is why tombs held statues.
  • Serdab = sealed room in a mastaba holding the ka statue of the dead (Djoser had one).
  • Mummification (about 70 days): remove the internal organs (the heart stays in the body for judgment), dry the body with natron salt, then wrap it in linen with amulets. Anubis is the god of this process.
  • Canopic jars = four jars for the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines, protected by the four sons of Horus.
  • Amulets = protective charms placed in the wrappings (for example the ankh, the scarab, the Eye of Horus).
  • Book of the Dead (originally "Coming Forth by Day"): prayers and spells on papyrus to protect the elite dead on the journey to the afterlife; a spell was placed between the legs.

Royalty, regalia, and symbols

  • How royalty is shown in sculpture: idealized, perfect, muscular, symmetrical bodies; rigid, upright, frontal pose; one foot forward; clenched fists; solid and permanent.
  • Regalia: nemes headdress, false royal beard, royal kilt, uraeus cobra, crook and flail, White Crown (Upper Egypt) and Red Crown (Lower Egypt).
  • Royal practices: "pharaoh" first meant "royal palace" (until about 1580 BCE). About 31 dynasties. Polygamous, harems, minor wives. To protect divine blood and keep power through the matrilineal line, the pharaoh married his sister, half sister or daughter, who became the Great Royal Wife. Menkaure and Khamerernebty were half siblings.
  • Papyrus and lotus: papyrus = Lower Egypt (north, the Delta); lotus = Upper Egypt (south). Shown together on Khafre's throne they mean the unity of the two lands.
  • Vulture and cobra on Tut's mask: vulture = Upper Egypt, uraeus cobra = Lower Egypt; both mean kingship.

New Kingdom people to know

  • Hatshepsut: wife and half sister of Thutmose II; no sons. Took the throne from her young stepson Thutmose III and declared herself pharaoh (1473 to 1458 BCE). Mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri has 3 levels with shrines to Amun, Hathor and Anubis. Shown in male royal regalia.
  • Ramses II: "last great warrior pharaoh," ruled 66 years. Rock cut temple at Abu Simbel (border of Nubia and Egypt): four 65 ft seated statues, Horus with sun disk in the middle, small female figures with Nubian features. Inside, 32 ft statues shown like Osiris. Moved about 700 ft in 1968 for the Aswan Dam. Principal wife Nefertari got her own temple.
  • Akhenaton (born Amenhotep IV): worshipped only Aton, the sun disk (monotheism). Body shown both male and female (swollen belly, curves) = Amarna style, from Tell el-Amarna. Priests were angry.
  • Nefertiti: principal wife, name means "the beautiful one is here," 6 daughters. Bust by the artist Thutmose.
  • Tiye: Akhenaton's mother, Nubian features, dramatic realism, mixed media (wood, gold, silver, alabaster, lapis).
  • Tutankhamen: tomb found in 1922 by British archaeologist Howard Carter, 4 intact rooms. Probably son of Akhenaton by a minor wife, ruled 10 years, died about 19. Three coffins; the innermost is solid gold (about 500 lb).

Ancient Nubia

  • Today's Sudan (North and South). Egyptians called upper Nubia Kush and the people Kushites.
  • Nubian kings ruled Egypt for almost 100 years as Dynasty 25 in the Late Period.
  • Royal capitals: Kerma, Gebel Barkal, Meroe, Napata. Gebel Barkal ("Holy Mountain") was the second capital (8th c. BCE), with a Temple of Amun (an Egyptian god in a Nubian temple = syncretism).
  • Sphinx of Taharqo (ruled 690 to 664 BCE, fought off the Assyrians): an Egyptian sphinx form with a Nubian king's face and a double uraeus (ruling both Egypt and Nubia) = syncretism.
  • Royal pyramids at Meroe: steeper, smaller pyramids; at least 40 generations of kings and queens buried there; painted tomb walls. The H shaped entrance structures are bekhanets (the Greeks called them pylons). Damaged with dynamite by a 19th century Italian explorer hunting treasure.

Essay prep: Part 3

Two Egypt images will be picked. For each, write a paragraph or two that hits all five methodology points, in this order. Tap a work to open its ready made outline.

Formula: 1. Subject (what it is, meaning, symbolism) · 2. Function/Purpose (why made, who saw it) · 3. Historical Context (period, patron, what was happening) · 4. Style (period or regional style) · 5. Formalism (use the vocabulary: composite view, hierarchal of scale, registers, relief, idealized, frontal, mixed media). Link ideas with transitions such as moreover, as a result, in contrast, for example, in addition, therefore, all in all.

From the Art Historical Methodologies sheet: Subject = identify and analyze the work in depth (what does it mean?). Function/Purpose = who viewed or interacted with it, and who was the intended audience? Historical Context = what life was like then: gender roles, political and religious practices, environment and geography, economic and class distribution, ethnicity, technology. Style = period/historical style or regional/geographical style. Formalism = accurate use of art history vocabulary.

Example in art history terms: "The Palette of Narmer shows the king striking an enemy. Moreover, he wears the White Crown of Upper Egypt. In contrast, the front shows him in the Red Crown of Lower Egypt. As a result, the palette is read as a symbol of political unification."

Placement tip: "Place and direction" words are perfect for describing an image: in the center, to the left, below, in the background.

MLA 9: Cite Right

From the ELAC Libraries video and the UNLV Works Cited handout. Good for an MLA quiz and for any paper in this class.

Core definitions

  • Citing = the formal way to give credit to sources (someone else's words, ideas or creations) used in academic work.
  • Four reasons to cite: 1) credit the scholars before us, 2) let readers follow up on sources, 3) make clear which ideas are yours and which are others', 4) show off your research skills. Also: to avoid plagiarism.
  • Plagiarism = using someone else's words, ideas or creations without proper credit and passing them off as your own. Breaks academic integrity. Consequences: fail the assignment, fail the class, or expulsion. (This class: a zero and a report to Academic Affairs.)
  • Example of plagiarism: paraphrasing a paragraph from a book about Hammurabi in your own words without a citation. Putting it in your own words does not remove the need to cite.
  • Always cite: summaries, paraphrases, direct quotes, and any graphs, charts, data or images you did not create.
  • Don't need to cite: common knowledge, meaning facts widely known and easily verified in multiple sources.

Style guides

StyleField
MLAEnglish and the Humanities
APAPsychology
ChicagoHistory and Fine Arts
ASASociology

Style guides cover citations, paper formatting, preferred language, and audience. Always ask your professor which style and edition. The MLA 9th edition came out in April 2021. Not much changed from the 8th, except accepted language such as using they/them for a single person.

Two kinds of citations

  • In text citation: in parentheses at the end of the sentence, with the author and page number, for example (Gardner 42). It points the reader to the full entry.
  • Works Cited: full citations on a new page at the end, titled Works Cited, double spaced, hanging indent (first line flush left, later lines indented), alphabetical by the first word (usually author's last name, or the title if there is no author).

Three steps to build a citation

  1. Figure out the source type (book, chapter, online article, interview...).
  2. Find the identifying info on the source: title, authors, date, location (page numbers for print, URL for online).
  3. Follow the style guide's format: watch punctuation, capitalization, spacing, italics, quotation marks.

Formulas and examples

Print book: Last, First. Title: Subtitle. Publisher, Year. (University Press shortens to UP.)

Marillier, Juliet. Blade of Fortriu. Tor Books, 2006.

Two authors: Last, First, and First Last. Three or more: Last, First, et al.

Scholarly article from a database: Last, First. "Article Title." Journal Title, vol. #, no. #, Year, pp. #‑#. Database, URL without https://.

Goldman, Anne. "Questions of Transport: Reading Primo Levi Reading Dante." The Georgia Review, vol. 64, no. 1, 2010, pp. 69‑88. JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/41403188.
  • Article titles go in quotation marks; book, journal and database names in italics.
  • Use vol., no., pp. (one page is p.).
  • Leave off https:// in MLA 9. Access dates are optional; check with your professor.
  • Ebook found online: add the database or ebook provider and URL.

Work of art (handy for this class): Artist Last, First. Title. Year, Museum, City.

Bearden, Romare. The Train. 1975, Museum of Modern Art, New York.

YouTube video: "Title." YouTube, uploaded by Name, Day Month Year, URL.

"Cite Right in MLA (9th Edition)." YouTube, uploaded by ELAC Libraries, www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ll5GGRaLeFA.

Every format from the UNLV Works Cited handout

The handout is based on the MLA 8th edition; citation formats are nearly identical in MLA 9.

SourceFormulaExample

Chapter 4 bonus: Prehistoric Aegean

Not listed on the Exam 1 guide, but it was in your files. Quick version.

  • Three regions: Cyclades = Cycladic; Crete = Minoan (named by Arthur Evans after King Minos); mainland = Helladic (Mycenaean).
  • Heinrich Schliemann (German, 19th c.) dug at Troy and Mycenae because of Homer's Iliad (about 750 BCE).
  • Cycladic marble figures: abstract, geometric, found in graves (Syros woman, Keros lyre player).
  • Knossos palace on Crete: no fortification wall; light wells; columns with wide bowl capitals that influenced Greek Doric. Paintings show bull leaping, ceremonies, nature and sea life with rich color.
  • Pottery terms: monochrome (1 color), bichrome (2, the octopus jar), polychrome (3 or more, Kamares ware).
  • Snake Goddess (faience): Earth Mother, snakes = regeneration and fertility, cat on head = control of nature.
  • Mycenae and Tiryns: fortified citadels. Passage types: post and lintel, corbeled arch ("house shape"), true arch. Lion Gate uses corbeling plus post and lintel. Treasury of Atreus is a tholos with a beehive vault.
  • Grave Circle A: gold funerary mask made by repoussé (hammering); inlaid dagger with lion hunt (syncretism with Assyrian hunts); shaft graves.
  • Warriors Vase (a krater): Mycenaean decline 1250 to 1200 BCE, then the Greek Dark Ages (1200 to 800 BCE).
